The statement is true, and I have a mathematical argument, but formalizing it in Lean 4 with Mathlib is more than I can finish here.

The sketch: let G(x) = ∫₀ˣ g. Since g > 0 and x²g(x) ≤ 1, G is strictly increasing and bounded on ℝ, with total range M < ∞. The gradient condition gives F_u/g(u) + F_v/g(v) = 0, so F is constant along the direction (1/g(u), 1/g(v)). That implies F(u,v) = h(G(v) − G(u)) for some function h with h(0) = 0 and bounded derivative on [−M, M]. Then |F(x_i, x_j)| ≤ K·|G(x_i) − G(x_j)|. Since the G-values of the n+1 points lie in an interval of length M, two of them are within M/n of each other, which gives the bound with C = K·M.

The hard parts in Lean are the level-set/ODE step (or an explicit inverse of G), a uniform bound on F that does not depend on how far the points are from 0, and the sInf/pigeonhole bookkeeping over `Fin (n+1)`.
